summary: Provides guidelines for using the SIP Caller Preferences extension. It demonstrates benefits through example applications, shows use cases, offers advice on registered feature tags and discusses problems. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you call someone, you can say which kind of device you would like to reach, such as video or a phone. This shows how to do it well.

questions: how to route sip calls by device type
subtitle: Guidelines showing how to use SIP caller preferences for device selection and call routing.

tldr.problem: When users have multiple devices (cell phone, work phone, home phone), callers need a way to specify which type of device they want to reach, not just hope for the best or maintain multiple phone numbers.
tldr.mechanism: SIP caller preferences extension (RFC 3841) allows callers to express preferences about device capabilities they want to reach, while devices register their capabilities. This document provides detailed examples and guidelines for using this mechanism correctly.
tldr.outcome: Callers can now request device types (video phone, mobile phone, voicemail), and the SIP proxy routes the call appropriately based on device capabilities. This document explains 19 real-world use cases and best practices for implementation.

today: SIP caller preferences remain an important mechanism for controlling call routing in VoIP deployments. The guidelines in RFC 4596 continue to guide implementors of SIP systems and VoIP applications that need device selection and preference-based routing capabilities. This document helped clarify and stabilize the specifications it builds on.

sections.title: Finding the Right Device
sections.content:
The SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) caller preferences extension allows callers to express preferences about how a call should be routed. This is particularly important because modern users have multiple communication devices: a cell phone, a work phone, a home phone, and one or more PC-based applications.

The challenge is that the called party (callee) may have different preferences for how their various devices should be contacted, and the calling party (caller) also has preferences about which device they want to reach. This document provides detailed guidelines for using the caller preferences extension (RFC 3841 and RFC 3840) with 19 real-world use cases demonstrating practical applications and implementation guidance.

The document helps implementors understand the matching algorithm, shows proper usage of feature tags, and provides best practices for handling complex scenarios like voicemail routing, multilingual support, and media capability negotiation.
sections.eli5: Today people have many ways you can contact them. This guide explains how to ask for the kind of device you want when you call, and how that works with the caller preference system.

sections.title: The One-Number Problem
sections.content:
In traditional telephone networks, each device has its own number, forcing users to give out multiple phone numbers on their business cards. When callers want to reach someone, they must decide which number to try, and if the person isn't there, try another number or hold.

The SIP caller preferences extension enables a better experience: a user can have a single address (the Address of Record, or AOR) and callers can select which device type they want to reach using a pull-down menu. To reach someone's cell phone, the caller selects their single address and then specifies "mobile phone". To reach them wherever they are, the caller just calls the address without specifying a device preference, and all devices ring simultaneously.

Another key use case is direct-to-voicemail: a busy executive can quickly leave a message by selecting a "leave voice message" option, which sends the call directly to voicemail instead of trying the person's phone first. Without caller preferences, this would require knowing the voicemail system's main number and extension.
sections.eli5: Instead of memorizing five different numbers for one person, you just need one number. You can then tell the system whether you want their cell, their office, or their voicemail. The system routes your call to the right device.

sections.title: Core Patterns from Real Use Cases
sections.content:
The document presents 19 detailed use cases showing how caller preferences work in practice. These cases demonstrate several core patterns:

  • Capability-based routing: INVITE requests route to phones (handling voice calls), while MESSAGE requests route to pagers (handling text messages), ensuring messages go only to devices that support them.
  • Package-based routing: SUBSCRIBE requests for presence information route to a presence agent, while SUBSCRIBE for dialog events and INVITE requests route to regular devices.
  • Media type selection: Callers requesting video connect to devices with video capability, while audio-only devices serve as a fallback. The "require" flag ensures the call fails rather than connecting to audio-only when video is essential.
  • Language preferences: Multi-lingual office staff register contacts with their language capabilities, and callers can specify which language they speak to reach the appropriate person.
  • Voicemail handling: Callers can prefer voicemail (direct-to-voicemail), explicitly avoid voicemail (require person-to-person), or accept voicemail as a fallback.
sections.eli5: These real examples show how the system handles different situations: calls for talking, messages for texting, video calls for people who have video, and calls in different languages to people who speak them.

sections.title: How Preference Matching Works
sections.content:
When a caller sends an INVITE request to a user's address, each registered device has a list of capabilities (feature tags) like "audio", "video", "methods='INVITE,MESSAGE'", and language preferences. The SIP proxy compares the caller's preferences (in Accept-Contact or Reject-Contact headers) against each device's capabilities.

The matching algorithm assigns scores: if a device's features match the caller's request perfectly, it gets a score of 1.0; partial matches get lower scores. The proxy then sorts devices by three criteria: the score from caller preferences, the device's q-value (set by the callee), and the order they were registered.

The "require" flag means that devices not matching the preference are discarded entirely (important when video is mandatory). The "explicit" flag means devices must actively declare the capability (important when the capability is rare or significant). Without these flags, non-matching devices are simply ranked lower.
sections.eli5: The system gives each device a score based on how well it matches what the caller wants. Better matches ring first. Special flags let you say "only ring devices that have this" or "ring them if they said they have it".

sections.title: Feature Tags and Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC defines when to use various feature tags that describe device capabilities. Mobility tags ("mobile" or "fixed") indicate whether the device is a cell phone or stationary phone. Methods tags list which SIP methods the device supports (INVITE for calls, MESSAGE for pages, SUBSCRIBE for subscriptions). Media tags ("audio", "video") indicate media types, and class tags ("personal", "business") indicate context.

Proper implementation requires that devices register all their capabilities accurately. If a device supports video but fails to register the video capability, a caller requesting video will not reach it, even though it could serve them. Multiple registrations from the same device are sometimes necessary when different feature sets need different preference values, such as registering one contact for English speakers at q=1.0 and another for Spanish speakers at q=0.5.

Some scenarios cannot be solved with caller preferences alone: for example, preferring voicemail but accepting a person as a fallback requires two separate call attempts (first try with voicemail required, then if that fails, try without preferences).
sections.eli5: Each device describes what it can do: "I speak English", "I have video", "I'm mobile", or "I can handle text messages". Callers say what they want, and the system matches them up. But you have to describe your device correctly or callers won't find you.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
This document includes detailed examples of the preference matching algorithm's implementation, showing how to extract feature sets from headers, compare value-ranges, and select contacts based on caller preferences. This guidance helps implementors avoid common mistakes.

Deployments must ensure that SIP user agents properly register their capabilities and that proxies correctly implement the matching algorithm from RFC 3841. Interoperability has been proven through extensive testing between implementations, though some corner cases (like contacts without any registered capabilities being "immune" from filtering) require careful handling.

The guidelines are informational, not standards-defining; this document explains how to use features defined in RFC 3840 (callee capabilities), RFC 3841 (caller preferences), and earlier specifications. It serves to clarify ambiguities and provide practical examples that helped refine the actual protocol specifications.
sections.eli5: This document is a how-to guide for programmers building SIP systems. It shows the math behind matching what the caller wants with what the device offers, and warns about gotchas they might miss.
